analysis.one_liner: Bans student lenders from paying colleges for loan business and forces clearer loan disclosures for students.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or floor vote in the Senate after its May 2007 referral, but Congress enacted similar student-loan conflict-of-interest rules later that same year.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have cracked down on the student loan industry's practice of paying colleges and financial aid officers for loan business. It banned lenders from offering gifts, trips, and payments to schools, barred schools from publishing "preferred lender" lists, required lenders to give students plain-language disclosures about rates, fees, and federal aid alternatives, and shut down programs letting schools themselves act as student lenders. It also ordered a federal review of whether private education loans are offered on discriminatory terms to lower-income students.
analysis.who_benefits: Students and parents taking out federal or private education loans. They would get written disclosures before signing—covering how the interest rate is set, all fees, default collection practices, and whether they qualify for cheaper federal aid instead—and would no longer be steered toward lenders that paid their school for the spot.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits guaranty agencies and lenders from offering colleges and financial aid employees premiums, payments, travel, and other inducements to win loan business, and disqualifies from the federal program any lender that makes such payments or consults for financial aid staff [S2][S3].

Requires lenders to give students written disclosures before issuing a loan, including that they may qualify for federal assistance instead, how the interest rate is determined, all fees, repayment benefits, collection practices on default, and whether their loans exceed the cost of attendance [S2][S3].

Bans schools from designating preferred lenders and requires them instead to make any lender's standardized loan terms available to all students, while telling students they may pick any lender they choose [S2][S3].

Requires every college to adopt and enforce a student loan code of conduct—with a signed annual attestation—and lets the Education Secretary limit, suspend, or terminate a school's federal loan program participation for violating it [S2][S3].

Sunsets the school-as-lender program on June 30, 2008, ending the arrangement in which colleges or their affiliates made federal student loans themselves, and terminates a lender's ability to serve as a school's trustee [S2][S3].

Directs the Education and Treasury Departments to review the private loan market for discriminatory lending patterns against students who qualify for a simplified financial aid application, and report recommendations for protection from predatory lending [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Student loan lenders and guaranty agencies in the federal Family Education Loan program, which lose paid access to schools and must carry new disclosure duties, and colleges that made money by acting as lenders or accepted lender perks, which lose that revenue and must write and enforce a code of conduct.
analysis.who_pays_short: Student lenders, guaranty agencies, and some colleges

drawbacks.text: The bill relies heavily on disclosure rather than price limits: it tells students what a loan costs and how the rate is set, but does nothing to cap the rates, fees, or default penalties themselves, so borrowers still bear the full cost of expensive loans [S2][S3].

It creates an exception letting schools certify private loans above federal borrowing limits for students who do not qualify for the simplified needs test, which could channel some students into costlier private borrowing rather than federal aid [S2][S3].

Colleges that ran school-as-lender programs lose that revenue stream; the bill softens this by allowing them to sell their existing loan portfolios only if all profits go to need-based grants at the school [S3].

The compliance burden is real for colleges: they must adopt a code of conduct, publish lender information, file a signed annual attestation signed by a senior officer, and risk losing federal loan program eligibility for willful violations [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections are genuine and targeted at a real problem—lenders paying for placement on school loan lists and aid officers taking lender perks—but they are mostly transparency rules, not price protections, so a student's loan itself would not get cheaper. The main cost falls on lenders, guaranty agencies, and school-lender programs, with a modest compliance load for all colleges and one provision that nudges some students toward private loans.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee in May 2007 and sat there until the Congress ended in January 2009, never reaching a committee vote or the Senate floor.

narrative.text: Senator Michael Enzi of Wyoming introduced the bill on May 2, 2007, joined by six other Republican senators as original cosponsors [S3][S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day; that referral was the last action ever recorded on the bill [S5].

The bill's list of cosponsors grew to seven Republicans, all in the minority party at the time, and no hearing, markup, or vote on the bill appears in its action history before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Students lost little in the end, because Congress enacted most of these same safeguards—a lender code of conduct, inducement bans, and the end of school-as-lender—in the College Cost Reduction and Access Act a few months later. The main thing that died with this bill was its sponsors' claim to the reform.

sides.party_line_note: All eight original sponsors were Republicans in the minority, and the Democratic-led committee never acted on it, so no vote ever revealed where the parties stood; the substance later passed in a separate 2007 law.

industries.note: The bill strips lenders of paid inducements, consulting deals with aid officers, and unsolicited application mailings used to win loan volume, and disqualifies violators from the federal program. Students benefit because loan choices are no longer steered by payments to their schools [S2][S3].

The bill bans guaranty agencies from offering premiums, payments, and travel to schools and lenders to secure their insurance role, bars mass unsolicited loan mailings to students, and prohibits doing schools' required work for free as a sweetener [S2][S3].

The bill sunsets the program letting institutions or their affiliates lend directly to their own students, closing a channel where the school deciding how much a student may borrow was also the lender profiting from it [S2][S3].

They face new written disclosure duties and lose the preferred-lender list as a marketing channel, but the bill also lets schools certify private loans above federal limits for some students, expanding where private loans can substitute for federal aid [S2][S3].
